items.title: Lindsay Clancy Makes Another Bid to Drop Murder Charges Before Retrial
items.summary:
Lindsay Clancy’s defense team has called on Massachusetts’ highest court to intervene ahead of her upcoming retrial in her latest bid to have her murder charges dropped.

In a petition filed Monday, November 16, with the state’s Supreme Judicial Court, Clancy’s lawyers asked to reverse Plymouth County Superior Court Judge William Sullivan’s recent denial of Clancy’s motion to dismiss the charges, per Boston.com . Sullivan’s decision cleared the way for a retrial.

The day of the petition’s filing, Sullivan scheduled Clancy’s second murder trial to take place on March 29, 2027.

Clancy, of Duxbury, sought to have the charges she’s facing in the killings of her three children dismissed on double jeopardy grounds after Sullivan declared a mistrial in her case on September 4.

Judge Denies Lindsay Clancy's Bid to Dismiss Case, Retrial Now a Possibility 

Clancy’s attorneys argue in their petition that she was “aggrieved” by Sullivan turning down her motion to dismiss on November 9.

“Respectfully, contrary to the trial court’s stated belief at the time, it did have viable choices other than declaring a mistrial,” her attorneys wrote in the filing.

They contend she “should not be ‘forced to run the gantlet’ again” after a deadlocked 11-1 jury couldn’t unanimously agree on whether she was criminally liable for the January 2023 deaths of her children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months.

Clancy’s defense team argues Sullivan should’ve investigated the lone holdout juror further after the jury foreperson alleged the man, Michael P. Desronvil , didn’t follow instructions…

He echoed in the caption, “MRI came back clean. No signs of a tumor and my brain is recovering great.”

Days prior, Amabile opened up about feeling nervous before undergoing his MRI.

“I’ve been feeling a little out of it the past couple days, but the weather is so nice I just went for a run. My first MRI from my surgery is next week, so I’m a little worried about that. But …” Amabile said in a November 11 Instagram Story as he shrugged his shoulders.

Amabile shared in July that he was preparing to undergo brain surgery after participating in a Prenuvo full body scan, which revealed a “blueberry size lesion.” Amabile underwent surgery in August and later revealed that he had been diagnosed with a “very low grade” astrocytoma — a type of brain or spinal cord tumor that may result in headaches, seizures, nausea or changes in mood or behavior, per the Mayo Clinic.

“They did get the whole thing,” he said in his video at the time. “When it comes to malignant brain tumors, they don’t know what’s left over, so I will be going on treatment, which is just a pill every day for the rest of my life to put the bad cells to sleep, and hopefully they stay asleep.”

items.title: JonBenet Ramsey's Dad Slams Claim Family Shouldn't Have Been Cleared in Case
items.summary:
JonBenét Ramsey’s dad, John Ramsey , fired back at Colorado prosecutor Michael Dougherty , who said he would not have ruled the family out as suspects if he had been overseeing the case when the 6-year-old pageant contestant was found dead in 1996.

“After 30 years, if they still think I am guilty, then please file charges, and we will settle this in court based on facts and evidence,” John, 82, told Fox News in a statement on Wednesday, November 18.

John continued, “They can’t selectively apply the unknown male DNA both ways. They have cleared a number of interesting suspects based on their DNA not matching unidentified male No. 1 DNA recovered from JonBenét’s person.”

John spoke out after the Boulder County District Attorney told local reporters that he “would not have” publicly ruled out JonBenét’s family as suspects like Mary Lacy , the prosecutor previously leading the case, did in 2008.

JonBenet Ramsey's 28-Year Murder Case Has Been 'Embarrassing' for Boulder PD 

“I’ve never ruled out people in a case that’s unsolved,” Dougherty said on November 10, according to The Boulder Daily Camera . “Doing right by the victim demands that I remain open-minded and committed to following the evidence wherever it leads.”

Dougherty added that Lacy’s public exoneration of the family likely didn’t harm the investigation because her conclusion was not legally binding.

JonBenét’s case gripped the nation after she was reported missing on December 26, 1996, with her family telling authorities that they found a ransom note demanding $118,000 for her safe return. She was tragically…

items.title: I saw how brightly stars like Russell Brand could shine, but there is darkness in the shadows | Sophie Heawood
items.summary:
After years of celebrity interviews, I have learned not to be fooled by the allure of fame. We never really know them – we know what they want us to know

As I sat in Southwark crown court, listening to the final day of Russell Brand’s trial, there was one subject that came up repeatedly, invoked as often by his defence as the prosecution. I don’t mean sex or coercion, but fame. It ran through every victim impact statement and loomed so large in the courtroom that it felt as if it was almost on trial itself.

I’m an entertainment journalist who has been covering celebrities for more than 20 years – as long as Brand has been one – and I have written about him at various stages of his career. But I went to Southwark crown court as a member of the public who wanted to see justice done. For the women he had hurt, for the ones who couldn’t get as far as the courtroom, and for all of us who came of age at a time when rape culture was so fast and furious that young women mistook it for a joke that we were in on. In the age of lads’ mags, sex felt cheapened, yet somehow we were the ones who ended up paying for this. So it was doubly strange to sit in court and feel somehow complicit in it - in how this media culture had encouraged Russell Brand.
